We can therefore say not only that every “person” is necessarily free and finite, and therefore historical, but also that every finite and free—that is, historical—being is necessarily a “person.”
So to say that a human being is an “individual” and to say that a human being is “synthetic,” or dialectical, is to say the same thing in different words.

That is why, once we have said that the human being is dialectical—that is, that human existence simultaneously contains all three dialectical aspects, thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—we can also say that the human being is a “free and historical person.”
To summarize, let us repeat the point once more.

In every form of human existence—whether in an individual person, in the human community as a whole, or even in any product of human activity—we can distinguish three aspects at work in the dialectic.
There is the thesis, in which “identity” predominates.
There is the antithesis, in which negativity predominates.
And there is the synthesis, in which “totality” predominates.
In reality, however, these aspects are inseparable.
The real human being is always a synthesis in the broad sense of the term. Human existence necessarily contains, alongside synthesis in the narrower sense, thesis and antithesis as well.

But as we have already seen, this real, general “synthesis” can itself function as a “thesis” in relation to another “synthesis” that plays the role of antithesis and, together with the thesis, produces a further synthetic synthesis.
In other words, every synthesis—every human existence or human entity, and everything made by human beings—can serve as the starting point of a dialectical process.
It can become a “thesis” that is abolished by an “antithesis” but preserved within a new “synthesis,” and so on.
When we speak about dialectic and dialectical existence, therefore, we have to approach the question from two different angles.
On the one hand, we can consider one and the same entity, or one and the same stage in its development over time.
From this perspective, the entity or stage is dialectical when it contains all three aspects—thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—simultaneously and in practice inseparably.

On the other hand, there can also be a dialectical relation between different entities, or between different stages in the development of one and the same entity. This relation allows us to arrange them in the order thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
In this case, the three can exist separately. They follow one another in time—in the kind of time ruled by the future, that is, by antithesis or “negativity.”
We will therefore call these entities dialectical as well, while calling the relation between them the real dialectic in the proper sense of the term.
We now know, at least to some extent, what the real dialectic described by the philosophical system of Hegelian Marxism—and in particular by Hegelian-Marxist Phenomenology—actually is.
We know that it is not a method but a reality.
And we also know that the philosophical method is nothing other than the method of giving a pure description of actuality.

If this description is “dialectical,” that is only because it reflects the dialectical structure of actuality with photographic precision, like a mirror. That structure exists in reality independently of its philosophical description.
If this is so—if the philosophical description of the real dialectic reflects its actual structure—then the description itself must also be divided along the two lines we have just distinguished.
Philosophy will describe, on the one hand, the dialectical aspects of actuality and, on the other hand, its dialectical stages: the dialectic in the proper sense, the real dialectic itself.
In actuality, as we know, the different aspects exist inseparably and simultaneously.
So if philosophy describes them separately, and even one after another, this is only because we cannot speak about everything at once or say everything in a single instant.
In this respect, the philosophical description of dialectical actuality does not, if you like, coincide perfectly with actuality itself.

But it differs from it no more than any description that unfolds in time while describing something whose parts exist simultaneously. It differs no more than a zoological description that talks first about a cat’s head, then about its torso, and so on.
Indeed, the difference is even smaller here.

For although the aspects of dialectic are simultaneous, they nevertheless possess an objective “logical” order. The “logical” antithesis “presupposes” the thesis, while the synthesis presupposes them both.
So when philosophy describes the different aspects of a phenomenon, it cannot choose an arbitrary order of presentation. It must arrange its descriptions as thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
The dialectical stages, by contrast, follow one another in time and can in fact be separated.
The thesis always appears before the antithesis, while the synthesis emerges only after the antithesis has appeared.
So the structure of the philosophical description of dialectical stages—or of dialectic itself—corresponds to the structure of the reality being described.
Even here, however, the correspondence may not be complete.

First, philosophy may take a thesis realized in the historical development of one entity and pair it with an antithesis taken from the historical development of another entity, even though an antithesis also appears in the first.
Philosophy does this when the second entity turns out to realize the antithesis in question “better”—more distinctly and more completely—than the first.
Second, as I have already noted, philosophy can depart somewhat from strict chronology when describing dialectical stages.
An antithesis is always generated after the thesis has appeared. But the antithesis often appears before the thesis has reached its full development.

And since philosophy naturally aims to describe a thesis in its fullest expression, it may describe a th†etical form that, in the form being described, emerges only after the phenomenon it identifies as the corresponding antithesis has already appeared.
But it is obvious that this departure from historical chronology is of no real importance and cannot count as a philosophical objection.
What, then, does it actually mean to describe dialectical aspects and stages?
We will understand this fully only when we encounter a concrete philosophical description—that is, the philosophical system as a whole.
But we can already say something about it here.
Suppose philosophy wants to describe the dialectical aspects of a particular individual, or a particular society, at a particular moment in its historical existence.
When describing that individual or society as a thesis, philosophy will emphasize everything that was “given” to it: everything it merely “inherited,” rather than what it personally made or created.
It will do this while provisionally acting as though it had forgotten that human beings can negate all of this—or even that they are already negating it in practice.

When speaking of the human being as an antithesis, by contrast, philosophy will notice everything that is new—and only what is new: everything that does not, so to speak, follow automatically from what had already been “given.”
It will instead assume that the human being freely negates this “given” reality, and therefore changes in an essential way—or at least possesses the possibility of such a change.
Finally, when speaking of the human being as a synthesis, philosophy will focus only on what has actually been realized out of this novelty: what has been generated by the negation of the given.
In other words, it will look at what has survived in this person, what has entered into them as a “fact” and has therefore itself become a new given.
Philosophy will then try to understand how and why this happened.
In studying the synthesis, therefore, philosophy tries to distinguish, within both thesis and antithesis, what has “stood the test” of actuality from what has “failed” that test.
It will try to identify what was “dead” in the given content of the thesis, and what was false theoretically or “utopian”—that is, false practically—in the creative project of the antithesis.
When philosophy describes the dialectic itself—that is, the dialectical stages—it proceeds according to the following principles.

Once it has identified some human-historical phenomenon that can be treated as a thesis, and therefore as the starting point of a historical development, philosophy knows that sooner or later this phenomenon will reach its “logical conclusion.”

That is, it will realize its “meaning” or, if you prefer, its “essence” as modified through time. It will reach what is “essential” within it. In other words, it will realize all the possibilities contained in that essence and compatible with that form of existence.
Philosophy will therefore describe the phenomenon at the moment when it actually reaches this “logical conclusion,” schematizing and “idealizing” it if necessary.
In doing so, philosophy knows that this phenomenon will eventually generate a new phenomenon opposed to it: something incompatible with it, yet related to it as non-A is related to A.
Philosophy will then try to find this opposing phenomenon in the actual world and describe it in its clearest form—again idealizing and schematizing it where necessary.

Finally, once it has established that the second phenomenon has abolished the first, philosophy will look for a third phenomenon that replaces them both, knowing in advance that it will contain traces of both the first and the second.
It will then describe this third phenomenon—again schematizing and idealizing it—precisely as a “third” form that unites the first two.
But in doing so, philosophy will also know that this third form will itself generate a new “negative” phenomenon.
It will therefore describe the third form as the starting point of a new historical process.
And it will continue in this way for as long as there remain phenomena that it has not yet described and that differ essentially from those it has already examined.

This is how philosophy in general proceeds when it describes dialectic. Phenomenology differs from Philosophy in the strict sense only in this: it describes dialectic not as it is “in truth,” but as it “appears” to human beings. In other words, it describes thesis, antithesis, and synthesis—both as aspects and as stages—as phenomena.

A phenomenon is reality as it appears to human beings. So the phenomenon itself is a human—or historical—appearance. For that reason, it too is dialectical. The same dialectical dependence therefore exists between phenomena as between the realities of which they are the phenomena. Thus, by describing the “appearances” of the dialectical stages, Phenomenology also describes the dialectical stages of the appearances themselves.

In other words, phenomenological description is just as “dialectical” as philosophical description, and for exactly the same reason. Why? Because what it describes is dialectical. Phenomenology is nothing more than the description of real dialectic considered as a series of “appearances”—that is, considered in its phenomenological aspect. Phenomenology is therefore neither more nor less than a complete phenomenological description of dialectic.

We have seen that the method of Phenomenology consists simply in the “pure description” of an object. This method allows us to choose the object, but also to schematize and idealize it. The chosen object is then described as it ought to be—that is, as it really would be if it developed and realized itself under conditions perfectly suited to it, conditions ideal for its development, without being distorted by accidental outside influences.

Schematizing and idealizing the chosen object therefore does not alter it in any essential way. In any case, the method adds nothing of its own. Every distinctive feature of the description comes entirely from the distinctive features of the object described—that is, from the real object of the description. In particular, as we have just seen, the “dialectical” character of the description comes entirely from the dialectical character of the object itself.

The dialectical character of the object described in Phenomenology therefore determines the distinctive character of phenomenological description—or, if one prefers, of the phenomenological “method.” We can define this method briefly by calling it “a posteriori deduction.”

To explain what this means, I will first describe the distinctive character of real dialectic. This character necessarily turns every description of dialectic into a “deduction” of this kind, without distorting dialectic in the process.

As we know, dialectic necessarily contains the “moment” of negativity: creative-and-negating action, or revolutionary action in the broad sense. This action is at the same time the effective expression of freedom or, more exactly, its realization.

This means that every dialectical being always appears as the result of a certain creative—and temporal—process or development. And precisely because it is dialectical, because it is a result, it can be understood or described only by understanding or describing the process through which it was created.

But this dialectical process is nothing other than the process by which a given being freely creates itself. In other words, the being is the result of its own negating activity and therefore of its creative, world-making, or free (“spontaneous”) activity.
Free activity—or an action whose process of development contains an element of freedom—differs from a necessary or “determined” process in only one respect: its result cannot be predicted.

Even if we knew the entire present and past of a dialectical being perfectly, this would not allow us to know its future. The future is not already “contained” within it. And it is not contained there because, however real the past and present of a given being may be, they do not determine its real future.
Freedom itself is precisely what is not in the present and was not in the past. It is the new element that seems to come from the future—that is, to come “from nothing.”

Freedom is neither being nor non-being. Yet in a certain sense it is real, because it is present within a real dialectical being. And insofar as it is real, freedom appears as the presence of nothingness within being and existence.
This entry of nothingness into what exists is precisely what we call free or creative action.
Clearly, then, freedom cannot be seen in what already is or what was. For that reason it cannot be foreseen or predicted on the basis of our knowledge of what exists or has existed.

But when freedom realizes itself in action—or as action, since outside action it does not exist—it becomes an element, a constituent part, of what is and exists. Once freedom has been realized and has entered existence, its real result—the result of a successful or completed action—can be known through knowledge of what exists.

And once we know this result, we also know its cause: the free action or “decision” without which the result could not have occurred. Yet before the result existed, this action itself neither was nor existed. It therefore could not have been an object of knowledge, since we can know only what exists or is.

Because the result of a free action or decision really exists, it has—like every reality—a concrete and positive content. So by knowing the result, we know not only that a certain action preceded it, but also what that action consisted in and what it was: namely, what it had to be in order to produce this particular result.

But every concrete action—that is, every action leading to a concrete result—also necessarily has a concrete starting point. So from our knowledge of the result and of the action that produced it, we can also discover this starting point.

And since everything that exists within a dialectical being is the result of free action, insofar as we are dealing with a dialectical being we must regard the “starting point” as discoverable. The being itself is the concrete result from which we can reconstruct the concrete action, the “starting point,” and so on.
Let us return to the example of the Rubicon.
On the night when Caesar was walking along the river, at the very moment of that walk, no one—neither Caesar himself nor anyone else—could know what decision he was going to make.
